q: {pundit}, you've won Le Mans, battled the endurance greats — what does a place like {trk} ask of a driver?
Be honest with me, {pundit} — how would a circuit like {trk} test YOU, back in your prototype days?
Take us back, {pundit} — you raced the endurance era's very best. What's the trick to {trk}?
{pundit}, from one champion to a room full of hopefuls — what's the secret this circuit demands?
You've felt places like {trk} at the limit in a prototype, {pundit}. What separates the quick from the rest here?
a: Honesty, {comm}. {trk} finds out anyone who lies to themselves about where the grip is. You have to drive the lap you've actually got, not the one you want.
Commitment in the fast stuff and patience in the slow stuff — and the discipline to never mix the two up. That's {trk} in one sentence.
It asks you the same question every lap, mate — how much do you trust the car? The drivers answering 'completely' are the ones at the top of the screen.
Rhythm. You can't bully {trk}, I tried for years. The moment you start forcing it, the lap time goes backwards.
A place like this tests the space between your ears more than your hands. Every mistake here breeds the next one — the trick is stopping the bleeding after one error, not three.
It would have tested me plenty, mate — circuits like {trk} punish greed. Take ninety-five percent every lap and the hundred-percent lap comes to you at the end.

q: You raced prototypes against Kristensen and McNish, {pundit}. Where's the lap really won at {trk}?
Drawing on all those Le Mans years, {pundit} — where would you be finding the time around {trk}?
{pundit}, put your engineer's hat on — where's the time hiding at {trk}?
For the viewers with the timing screens open, {pundit} — which part of {trk} decides the lap?
One sector to get right at {trk}, {pundit} — which one and why?
a: The slow corners, {comm}, always the slow corners. Everyone's flat where it's easy to be flat — the lap lives where the car is hardest to place.
Corner exit onto the longest straight — that's the only overtaking currency there is. Sacrifice the entry, get the exit, bank the time all the way down the straight.
Wherever the track drops away and your brain says lift — that's where it's won. The ones who keep their foot in through there gain for free.
Braking, mate. Not the latest braker — the one who's off the brakes EARLIEST and back to throttle first. It looks slower and it's quicker.
The corner nobody talks about. Every circuit has a glamour corner and a money corner, and they're never the same one.
It's won in the head on lap one and in the tyres on the last lap. In between you're just trying not to give it away.

q: {pundit}, with a Le Mans crown to your name — how does this lot compare to the WEC legends you raced?
You shared a track with Kristensen, Pirro, McNish, {pundit}. Anyone out there today remind you of them?
Honest answer, {pundit} — would the greats you raced against be beating this field?
Measure this grid against your era, {pundit} — better, worse, or just different?
{pundit}, you knew what the very best looked like from six inches behind them. See anything like it out there today?
a: There are flashes, {comm}. What made Kristensen special wasn't speed — everyone was fast — it was that he never had a bad Tuesday. Consistency was the superpower. A couple out there are learning that.
Different animals, mate. We managed cars for hours; these drivers sprint from lights to flag. But class is class in any era — you can see it in how calm the quick ones look.
The greats would be at the front here too, no question — but they'd have to work for it harder than people think. The overall level today is frighteningly high.
What I look for is what McNish had — total aggression under total control. Sounds like a contradiction. When you see a driver make it look calm AND fast, that's the lineage.
Some of these would have survived our era, and I mean that as a real compliment — ours ate people alive. The ones who take care of the car while pushing? They'd have thrived.
You never compare eras straight up, {comm}, you compare gaps. How far ahead of your teammate are you in the same car? The greats were always half a second clear. Watch for that out there.

q: {pundit}, endurance racing is a different discipline — what did those Le Mans years teach you that sprint racing never could?
Twenty-four hours flat out, {pundit} — what does that actually do to a driver's mind?
What's the one endurance-racing habit you wish every sprint driver out there had, {pundit}?
You did triple stints at Le Mans in the dark, {pundit}. What did that teach you about yourself?
{pundit} — sprint drivers chase the perfect lap, endurance drivers chase what, exactly?
a: Patience as a weapon, {comm}. In endurance racing the race comes TO you if you're still there at the end. Half the battles you see out there today don't need fighting.
It teaches you that the car is a teammate, not a tool. Abuse it in hour two and it abandons you in hour twenty-two. The drivers out there being kind to their tyres learned that lesson somewhere.
Lift before the kerb, mate. One habit. The kerb takes a hundredth and pays you back with a broken damper at the worst possible moment.
The dark stints teach you the difference between fear and information. Your body screams all night — you learn to hear only the messages that matter. That skill wins races in any discipline.
The perfect AVERAGE, {comm}. Anyone can do one great lap. Doing a hundred good ones in a row, that's the endurance art — and honestly, that's what wins sprint races too.
That speed is a decision, not a talent. At three in the morning at Le Mans nobody's talented — the ones still quick are the ones who DECIDED to be. You can see who's decided out there today.

q: {pundit}, you did this in anger for twenty years — what's the one thing the onboard cameras never show you?
For everyone watching at home, {pundit} — what does it actually FEEL like out there that the TV can't convey?
The broadcast makes it look smooth, {pundit}. What's the reality inside the cockpit?
{pundit}, what would surprise people most if they could sit in that car for a single lap?
Tell the truth, {pundit} — how violent is it really, out there?
a: The violence, {comm}. TV smooths everything. A 'gentle' lap out there is your head slamming the headrest, hands fighting the wheel every metre, and a fire behind you making noise you feel in your teeth.
How BUSY it is. On television a straight looks like a rest. In the car a straight is where you're checking dashes, managing switches, planning the next three corners — the rest never comes.
The heat, mate. Nobody talks about the heat. An hour in that cockpit and you've lost two kilos. The last ten laps aren't a driving contest, they're a fitness one.
How much the car moves. From the outside it looks on rails. From the seat it's alive under you every single corner — the skill isn't stopping the movement, it's letting it happen without panicking.
The margins. From the couch a metre looks like nothing. At three hundred an hour a metre is your whole life. What these drivers do casually would terrify a normal person into next week.
The silence in your head when it's going well. Sounds odd — but the great laps are quiet, everything slows down. The moment the lap gets loud in your mind, you're already slow.

q: {pundit}, you've been on both ends of the radio — what makes a great race engineer, from the driver's seat?
When you were mid-battle at Le Mans, {pundit}, what did you actually WANT to hear from the pit wall?
{pundit} — how much of a driver's race is really decided by the voice in their ear?
Best thing an engineer ever said to you in a race, {pundit}?
And the radio, {pundit} — friend or distraction when you're at the limit?
a: Economy, {comm}. A great engineer gives you the one number that changes what you do next, and nothing else. The bad ones narrate. The good ones inform.
Silence, mostly! When it mattered — one calm sentence. If the voice in your ear is calm, you're calm. Engineers set the driver's heart rate, they don't just set the strategy.
More than the viewers ever know. A good engineer places you in gaps you can't see, wins you positions in the pit window. I'd say two or three positions a race live and die on that radio.
'He's struggling more than you are.' Middle of the night, Le Mans, me hanging on by a thread — and that one line put me back in the fight. The best radio calls are psychology, not data.
A friend with strict visiting hours, mate. In the braking zone, nobody speaks — that's sacred. On the straight, tell me everything. Engineers who understand that timing are worth gold.
Everything, honestly. Drivers get the trophies but the race is a duet. When it clicks between a driver and their engineer you can hear it — the whole car sounds more decisive.

q: You raced Schumacher and Häkkinen for a title, {comm}. Does this lot have what those greats had?
You raced wheel to wheel with Schumacher, {comm}. Does anything on this grid remind you of him?
Straight question, {comm} — anyone out there today you'd have worried about in your championship year?
You've seen greatness from a car length away, {comm}. Spot any of it on this grid?
{comm}, does anyone out there have that thing Mika had — whatever it was?
a: What Michael had, {pundit}, was relentlessness — every lap of every session attacked like it was for the title. And yes, I see one or two out there driving in-laps like they matter. That's the tell.
Mika's gift was silence under pressure — you'd throw everything at him and get nothing back, no wobble, no mistake. Watch the leaders here under pressure; the ones who go QUIETER are the real ones.
One or two would have worried me, honestly. Not for their speed — everyone's fast — for their decision-making. The greats made the right call at two hundred miles an hour, every time.

Greatness looks boring from the outside, mate — that's the secret. No drama, no hero saves, just lap after lap exactly where they intend. There's some suspiciously boring driving at the front today, and I mean that as high praise.
The thing Mika had was that he only showed you his real pace when it counted. Sandbagger of the century! So ask me again in the final five laps — that's when you find out who's got it.
They're missing the fear, {pundit}, and I envy them for it. We drove circuits that punished mistakes with hospitals. But raw craft? Some of these would have lived with us, no question.

q: {comm}, you won a world championship — what does a title fight actually do to a driver, week after week?
Take us inside it, {comm} — the pressure of a championship run. What's it really like?
{comm}, the season your title went to the wire — how did you sleep?
What's the moment you knew you were going to be champion, {comm}?
Championship pressure, {comm} — does it make you faster or slower?
a: It shrinks your whole life to a points table, {pundit}. You brush your teeth thinking about the gap. The skill isn't handling the car — it's handling the maths without letting it drive for you.
Everyone imagines it's fear of losing. It isn't — it's the exhaustion of never being allowed an ordinary day. Champions aren't the fastest, they're the ones with the deepest reserves in November.
Sleep? Ha! I didn't sleep from summer onwards. You lie there running scenarios — what if it rains, what if I DNF. The title's won at three in the morning as much as on Sunday afternoon.

There wasn't one moment — that's the honest answer. There was a Tuesday, mid-season, when I stopped checking the standings. The moment you stop counting is the moment you're actually quick enough to win it.
Faster, if you let it. Pressure is just fuel with bad PR. The ones it slows down were never going to be champions — the ones it sharpens, you can see it from the grandstands.
It changes how you race everyone else, {pundit}. Suddenly there are drivers you CANNOT crash with and points you cannot risk. Racing with a calculator in your head — that's the real test.

q: {comm}, you won a world title and then went and threw yourself down forest roads for fun. Explain yourself.
F1 champion turned rally man, {comm} — why on earth did you do it?
{comm}, you were World Champion before you ever went rallying — bet the forests were a culture shock?
What did rallying teach a Formula One world champion, {comm}?
Circuit racing versus the stages, {comm} — which one is the truer test?
a: Because the title answered every question except one, {pundit} — could I drive, or could I just drive THAT? The forests don't care about your CV. Best decision I ever made, and the most humbling.

I wanted to be a beginner again, honestly. When you've reached the top of one mountain you either defend the view or find a taller mountain. Gravel at a hundred and forty through trees? Taller mountain.

Culture shock doesn't cover it! In F1 I knew every bump for a decade. In rally the road is a stranger doing its best to kill you, and your only friend is a voice reading pace notes. I loved it beyond reason.

That grip is a rumour, mate! Circuit racing teaches you to use grip; rallying teaches you to live happily without it. Every save you see me admire on this broadcast — that's the rally education talking.

They test different organs, {pundit}. Circuits test the head — precision, repetition. The stages test the heart — commitment into the unseen. The complete driver needs both, and I got to fail at both spectacularly.
The stages taught me that the car is never truly under control — you're just negotiating. Once you accept that, funnily enough, you're faster everywhere. Even on a billiard-table circuit like this.

q: Come on, {comm} — one lap in your old Grand Prix car versus the modern stuff. Where's your money?
Your championship car against today's machinery, {comm} — honestly, which is faster where it matters?
{comm}, would today's drivers cope with what you drove, and would you cope with theirs?
Miss the old cars, {comm}, or is that just nostalgia doing its work?
Modern racing versus your era, {comm} — better, or just different?
a: The modern car takes the lap time, no argument — physics moved on. But put both on a damp track with worn tyres and I'll back the old warrior, because MY car demanded a driver and today's cars merely request one.
Today's car is faster everywhere, {pundit}, and I'd still choose mine. Lap time isn't the only measurement — my car frightened me every single day, and I miss being frightened.

They'd cope with ours after a week of respect and one big scare — talent transfers. Me in theirs? Give me a month. The speed I'd manage; it's trusting the grip I'd have to learn. My instincts say 'lift' where these cars say 'flat'.

Of course it's nostalgia — and nostalgia is underrated! But here's what's real: our cars showed you the driver working. If some of that visible struggle came back, nobody would change channel, put it that way.
The racing today is closer and the driving is better — I'll say it plainly. What we had was consequence, and consequence made legends. Different currencies, {pundit}. Both valuable.
My money's on the modern car and my heart's in the old one — and if those ever agree with each other, I'll retire from this booth on the spot.

q: {comm}, F1 champion turned rally man — what does {trk} take, in your book?
From a world title to the rally stages, {comm} — how would you be tackling {trk}?
Your read on this circuit, {comm} — what's {trk} really asking of them today?
{comm}, you've raced everything with wheels — where does a place like {trk} rank as a test?
One piece of advice for every driver out there at {trk} right now, {comm} — go.
a: Precision first, bravery second — most drivers get that ordering wrong, {pundit}. {trk} pays you for being boringly accurate for ninety percent of the lap so you can be brave where it counts.

I'd be treating it like a rally stage, honestly — learn where the track FORGIVES you before spending anything where it doesn't. Every circuit has a corner that lets you off. Find it, use it, bank the rest.

It's asking for honesty about the brakes. Watch the good ones — the braking is where {trk} sorts the field, and the trick is doing it straight, calm and slightly early. Drama into the corner is time out of it.
Higher than people think. The famous circuits get the poetry, but a lap of {trk} done properly requires everything in the toolbox. There's nowhere to hide out there today.
Stop steering so much! That's my advice for half this field. The fewer inputs you make at a place like this, the faster it goes. The steering wheel is for requests, not arguments.
Respect it for three laps, then attack it forever. The drivers who go the other way round — brave early, careful late — are the ones we'll be talking about for the wrong reasons.

q: {comm}, hand on heart — is calling the race harder or easier than driving it?
Do you miss it terribly when you watch them go wheel to wheel, {comm}?
{comm}, what do you see from up here that you never saw from the cockpit?
Be honest, {comm} — do your hands still move when they go through the fast stuff?
If they gave you one race back, {comm} — which one and why?
a: Easier on the body, harder on the soul, {pundit}. In the car you can DO something about what's going wrong. Up here I can only describe it — beautifully, of course.
Every single lap, mate. It fades to a hum most days — then someone pulls a move like we saw earlier and the hum becomes a roar. You never stop being a racing driver. You just stop being paid for it.

The whole story at once — that's the gift of the booth. In the car your race is three metres of track and one mirror. Up here I watch twenty stories collide in real time. Honestly, it's a better view. Don't tell the drivers.
They're moving right now, {pundit}! Left hand's been dancing since the green flag. My wife says I drive the whole race from the sofa on Sundays too. No apologies.
The one I lost, obviously — champions never replay the wins. There's a race from my title year I've re-driven ten thousand times in my head, and I win it in all of them. That's retirement for you.
